audit.title: Security audit
audit.more_items: … and {n} more (all of them are in the exported report)
audit.counts: {ok} good · {warn} could be better · {fail} bad · {unknown} not checked · {info} informational
audit.run_as_admin: Some checks need admin: run Mapache as Administrator for a complete result.
audit.bitlocker_banner: Without BitLocker, anyone who gets your disk (theft, loss, booting from a USB) can read everything, including hiberfil.sys, pagefile.sys and memory dumps. It's the first thing worth fixing.
audit.threat_model: This protects you from common malware, device theft and attacks on shared networks. No configuration protects against a nation-state or agency targeting you.
audit.bitlocker.title: BitLocker on the system drive
audit.bitlocker.why: Without encryption, whoever gets the disk (theft, loss, booting from USB) reads all your files, browser sessions and memory artifacts. With TPM only, the disk unlocks by itself at power-on: a startup PIN closes attacks like TPM sniffing.
audit.bitlocker.fix: Turn on BitLocker (Windows Pro) or Device encryption (Home) and keep the recovery key off the PC. Paranoid level: TPM + startup PIN (Hardening will guide you).
audit.bitlocker.off: OFF: the disk is not encrypted
audit.bitlocker.suspended: suspended: the disk is encrypted but unlocks without protection
audit.bitlocker.on_unknown_pin: on (without admin it can't tell whether it uses a PIN)
audit.bitlocker.pin: on with a startup PIN or key
audit.bitlocker.tpm_only: on with TPM only (no startup PIN)
audit.secureboot.title: Secure Boot
audit.secureboot.why: Prevents an unsigned bootloader or bootkit from starting before Windows (malware no antivirus sees because it loads first).
audit.secureboot.fix: Enable it in the PC's UEFI (BIOS) settings. Many modern anti-cheats require it too.
audit.secureboot.legacy: not available (legacy BIOS boot or not reported)
audit.tpm.title: TPM chip
audit.tpm.why: Stores BitLocker, Windows Hello and Credential Guard keys so they can't be copied off the disk.
audit.tpm.fix: Enable the TPM (fTPM on AMD, PTT on Intel) in the UEFI settings.
audit.dma.title: Kernel DMA protection
audit.dma.why: Stops a plugged-in Thunderbolt/USB4 device from reading memory directly (physical attacks that take seconds).
audit.dma.fix: Depends on the firmware: enable IOMMU / AMD-Vi / VT-d in UEFI. If your PC has no Thunderbolt/USB4 the risk is low.
audit.vbs.title: Core isolation (VBS / memory integrity)
audit.vbs.why: Memory integrity (HVCI) blocks loading vulnerable or malicious drivers into the kernel, a common technique of malware and some cheats.
audit.vbs.fix: Windows Security → Device security → Core isolation. NOTE: VirtualBox switches to Hyper-V and gets slower (your Kali/Parrot VMs), and some anti-cheats or old drivers fail.
audit.credguard.title: Credential Guard
audit.credguard.why: Isolates LSASS credentials in a virtualized environment: tools like mimikatz can no longer pull them from memory.
audit.credguard.fix: Requires Windows Pro/Enterprise and VBS. It will be enabled from Hardening (advanced level), with the same VirtualBox warning.
audit.lsa_ppl.title: LSA protection (RunAsPPL)
audit.lsa_ppl.why: Makes LSASS a protected process: not even an administrator can read its memory to steal hashes and tickets.
audit.lsa_ppl.fix: Windows Security → Core isolation → Local Security Authority protection. Medium risk: some old drivers and anti-cheats fail.
audit.wdigest.title: WDigest (plaintext passwords in memory)
audit.wdigest.why: With UseLogonCredential=1 Windows keeps your password in plaintext in LSASS. Malware turns this on on purpose.
audit.wdigest.fix: Set UseLogonCredential to 0 or delete the value (Hardening will do it). If you didn't set it, check the PC.
audit.def_rtp.title: Antivirus and real-time protection
audit.def_rtp.why: It is the main defense against infostealers, trojans and ransomware that come in cracks, mods and downloads.
audit.def_rtp.fix: Turn on real-time protection in Windows Security. If a tool disabled it (some “optimizers” and debloaters do), revert that change.
audit.def_rtp.off: Defender is not protecting (mode: {mode}) and there is no other antivirus
audit.def_rtp.unreadable: could not read Defender's status (disabled or removed?) and there is no other antivirus
audit.def_sigs.title: Antivirus signatures up to date
audit.def_sigs.why: Old signatures don't recognize recent malware, which is exactly what circulates on Discord and crack sites.
audit.def_sigs.fix: Windows Security → Virus protection → Check for updates. If they never update, check Windows Update.
audit.def_tamper.title: Tamper protection
audit.def_tamper.why: Stops a program (even with admin) from turning Defender off or adding exclusions: it's the first thing malware tries.
audit.def_tamper.fix: Windows Security → Virus protection → Manage settings → Tamper protection.
audit.def_excl.title: Defender exclusions
audit.def_excl.why: An exclusion is a folder, process or extension Defender doesn't scan. Adding exclusions is the first move of many infostealers and miners, and crack tutorials ask you to do it.
audit.def_excl.fix: Review each exclusion in Windows Security → Manage settings → Exclusions and delete the ones you don't recognize. If you excluded your pentest tools, limit it to that exact folder.
audit.def_excl.suspicious: {n} suspicious exclusion(s): user folders, whole drives, interpreters or executable extensions
audit.def_asr.title: Attack surface reduction (ASR) rules
audit.def_asr.why: They block typical malware behavior: Office spawning processes, obfuscated scripts, LSASS credential theft, rare downloaded executables…
audit.def_asr.fix: Hardening will enable them, audit mode first. Medium risk: they can block dev or pentest tools.
audit.def_pua.title: Potentially unwanted app (PUA) blocking
audit.def_pua.why: Stops adware, bundled miners and “installers” that bring junk software.
audit.def_pua.fix: Windows Security → App & browser control → Reputation-based protection → Potentially unwanted app blocking.
audit.fw.title: Windows Firewall
audit.fw.why: Without a firewall, any service listening on your PC is exposed to the network (critical on public wifi or at university).
audit.fw.fix: Turn on the firewall for all profiles and keep “block inbound connections” as default.
audit.fw.ok: on for all profiles, blocks inbound by default
audit.fw.allow: allows inbound connections by default in: {profiles}
audit.smb1.title: SMBv1
audit.smb1.why: A 1984 protocol with no encryption or signing. WannaCry and NotPetya spread through it (EternalBlue).
audit.smb1.fix: Turn off the “SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support” feature (Hardening will do it).
audit.smb_sign.title: Required SMB signing
audit.smb_sign.why: Without signing, an attacker on the network can relay your authentication to another machine (NTLM relay) or tamper with traffic.
audit.smb_sign.fix: Require signing on client and server (RequireSecuritySignature=1). Windows 11 24H2 already does by default.
audit.llmnr.title: LLMNR (multicast name resolution)
audit.llmnr.why: When a name isn't in DNS, Windows asks the whole local network. Responder (like in CTFs) answers “it's me” and receives your password's NetNTLMv2 hash.
audit.llmnr.fix: Disable it with the “Turn off multicast name resolution” policy (EnableMulticast=0). Hardening will do it.
audit.netbios.title: NetBIOS over TCP/IP (NBT-NS)
audit.netbios.why: Same as LLMNR: another broadcast mechanism Responder poisons to capture hashes.
audit.netbios.fix: Disable it on each adapter (NetbiosOptions=2). Only networks with very old machines need it.
audit.rdp.title: Remote Desktop (RDP)
audit.rdp.why: Exposed RDP is one of the most common ransomware entry points (brute force and bugs like BlueKeep).
audit.rdp.fix: Turn it off if you don't use it. If you need it, require NLA and only use it through a VPN (e.g. Tailscale).
audit.remotereg.title: Remote Registry
audit.remotereg.why: Lets the registry be read and changed over the network; useful to an attacker who already has credentials.
audit.uac.title: User Account Control (UAC)
audit.uac.why: UAC is what forces a program to ask before getting admin. Without it, any malware you run gets full control.
audit.uac.fix: Raise it to “Always notify” (ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=2) with the secure desktop. Hardening will do it.
audit.uac.always: always asks on the secure desktop
audit.uac.no_secure_desktop: no secure desktop: another program could fake the click
audit.uac.default: default level (Windows' own changes don't prompt; known bypasses exist)
audit.smartscreen.title: SmartScreen for apps and files
audit.smartscreen.why: Warns before running a downloaded program that almost nobody has used or that's known to be malicious.
audit.smartscreen.fix: Windows Security → App & browser control → Reputation-based protection. Some debloaters turn it off.
audit.psv2.title: PowerShell 2.0
audit.psv2.why: PowerShell 2.0 has no AMSI or script logging: malware calls it (powershell -version 2) to dodge the antivirus.
audit.psv2.fix: Turn off the “Windows PowerShell 2.0” feature (Hardening will do it). Nothing modern needs it.
audit.psv2.maybe: the 2.0 engine seems installed: confirm as admin
audit.pslog.title: PowerShell script block logging
audit.pslog.why: Records what PowerShell runs (already deobfuscated) in Event Viewer: without it, after an infection there's no trace of what it did.
audit.pslog.fix: Enable it with the ScriptBlockLogging policy (Hardening will do it). Useful for your DFIR practice.
audit.sysmon.title: Sysmon (advanced event logging)
audit.sysmon.why: Free Microsoft tool that logs processes, connections and changes in detail. Optional.
audit.sysmon.fix: Install it from Sysinternals with a known config (e.g. SwiftOnSecurity or Olaf Hartong).
audit.wu.title: Windows Update
audit.wu.why: Most real attacks use vulnerabilities that already have a patch. An unpatched PC is the easy target.
audit.wu.fix: Settings → Windows Update → Check for updates. If a debloater (e.g. AtlasOS) paused or disabled them, turn them back on.
audit.wu.service_off: the Windows Update service is DISABLED
audit.wu.old: the last installed update ({kb}) is {days} days old
audit.autorun.title: AutoRun
audit.autorun.why: When a USB or disc is plugged in, Windows may offer to open content automatically: a classic USB worm vector.
audit.autorun.fix: Disable it for all drives (NoDriveTypeAutoRun=255). Hardening will do it.
audit.guest.title: Guest account
audit.guest.why: An account without a password anyone can use on the PC or over the network.
audit.admins.title: Administrator accounts
audit.admins.why: Using an admin account daily means whatever you run is one UAC click away from owning the PC. A standard account for daily use greatly limits damage.
audit.admins.fix: Create a standard account for daily use and keep the admin one for installing. Check there are no extra admins.
audit.admins.daily: your daily account is an administrator
audit.lock.title: Inactivity lock
audit.lock.why: If you step away and leave the PC unlocked, anyone walking by gets your session (Discord, browser, Steam).
audit.lock.fix: Set a lock after 15 minutes or less (and get used to Win+L).
audit.lock.none: no automatic lock configured (only on sleep)
audit.office_macros.title: Office macros
audit.office_macros.why: Documents with macros are still a typical infection vector (attachments, downloaded “assignments”).
audit.office_macros.fix: Don't enable “all macros” and keep blocking macros in files from the internet.
audit.mem.encrypted: protected because BitLocker encrypts the disk
audit.mem.no_bitlocker: WITHOUT BitLocker anyone with the disk can read it
audit.hiber.title: Hibernation (hiberfil.sys)
audit.hiber.why: hiberfil.sys is a copy of RAM: it can contain passwords, keys and open sessions. Forensic tools like Volatility read it.
audit.hiber.fix: What really matters is BitLocker. If you don't hibernate: powercfg /h off. To keep fast startup with a smaller file: powercfg /h /type reduced.
audit.pagefile_clear.title: Clear the pagefile at shutdown
audit.pagefile_clear.why: pagefile.sys holds chunks of memory that don't fit in RAM, secrets included. Without encryption they stay on disk after shutdown.
audit.pagefile_clear.fix: With BitLocker it isn't needed. Without it: ClearPageFileAtShutdown=1 (shutdown gets slower).
audit.crashdump.title: Memory dump type
audit.crashdump.why: After a blue screen, Windows may save all kernel memory (or all RAM) to disk, with whatever it contains.
audit.crashdump.fix: Use “small dump” (CrashDumpEnabled=3): still useful for diagnosis and holds almost no data.
audit.dumps_present.title: Memory dumps on disk
audit.dumps_present.why: The .dmp files in LiveKernelReports, Minidump or MEMORY.DMP are real system memory: they may hold secrets and take a lot of space.
audit.dumps_present.fix: If you don't need them for diagnosis, delete them with “Free up space” → Memory dumps.
audit.persist.lolbin: uses a Windows binary the way malware does (LOLBin)
audit.persist.unsigned_user_dir: in a user-writable folder without a valid signature ({sig})
audit.persist.missing_n: {n} of {m} point to files that no longer exist
audit.run_entries.title: Programs that start at sign-in (Run and Startup folder)
audit.run_entries.why: It's the persistence method most used by infostealers and RATs: that's how they run again every time you sign in.
audit.run_entries.fix: Review the list. Anything you don't recognize, look it up (name + path) and check the file on VirusTotal before deleting. If it's malware, change your passwords and sign out sessions from another device.
audit.tasks.title: Third-party scheduled tasks
audit.tasks.why: Scheduled tasks let malware run periodically or at boot, even as SYSTEM.
audit.tasks.fix: In Task Scheduler, review those pointing to AppData, Temp or ProgramData or using powershell/mshta, and disable the ones you don't recognize.
audit.services.title: Services in user-writable folders
audit.services.why: A service runs as SYSTEM: if its executable is where any program can write, replacing it gives full control.
audit.services.fix: If you don't recognize the service, investigate it. If it's legitimate, the installer is at fault: reinstall it to Program Files.
audit.unquoted.title: Unquoted service paths
audit.unquoted.why: With “C:\Program Files\My App\svc.exe” unquoted, Windows tries C:\Program.exe first: whoever can write there runs code as SYSTEM. Classic privesc (you'll see it in HTB/OSCP).
audit.unquoted.fix: Fix the service's ImagePath by adding quotes (or update the program; it's an installer bug).
audit.wmi.title: WMI event subscriptions
audit.wmi.why: “Fileless” persistence used by advanced malware: WMI runs a command or script when an event happens.
audit.wmi.fix: Investigate each consumer (Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/subscription). Almost no legitimate consumer software uses them.
audit.wmi.found: {n} consumer(s) that run commands or scripts
audit.ifeo.title: Executable hijacking (IFEO / SilentProcessExit)
audit.ifeo.why: A “Debugger” value makes another program run instead when you open one (e.g. pressing Shift 5 times at the sign-in screen).
audit.ifeo.fix: If you didn't set it (some tools like Process Explorer use it to replace Task Manager), delete it.
audit.appinit.title: AppInit_DLLs
audit.appinit.why: Loads a DLL into almost every GUI program: an old rootkit and adware technique.
audit.appinit.fix: Empty AppInit_DLLs and set LoadAppInit_DLLs=0 unless software you recognize needs it.
audit.appinit.on: ACTIVE: a DLL is loaded into programs
audit.appinit.dormant: DLLs are configured but loading is disabled
audit.winlogon.title: Sign-in (Winlogon Shell / Userinit)
audit.winlogon.why: Changing Shell or Userinit makes malware start with the desktop, before almost everything else.
audit.winlogon.fix: Restore Shell = explorer.exe and Userinit = C:\Windows\system32\userinit.exe, and scan the PC.
audit.hosts.title: Hosts file
audit.hosts.why: Malware edits it to block antivirus updates or to redirect sites (banks, Steam) to fake servers.
audit.hosts.fix: Check C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts and delete the lines you didn't add.
audit.hosts.blocks: {n} block(s) (typical of privacy lists or a debloater)
audit.proxy.title: System proxy
audit.proxy.why: A configured proxy can see and modify your web traffic. Some malware sets one to steal sessions.
audit.proxy.fix: If it's not yours (Burp, mitmproxy, a work VPN), turn it off in Settings → Network → Proxy.
audit.rootcerts.title: Root certificates added by the user
audit.rootcerts.why: A root certificate lets whoever controls it impersonate any HTTPS site. Burp, Fiddler and mitmproxy install one; so does malware.
audit.rootcerts.fix: If it's from your pentest tools, remove it when not in use (certmgr.msc → Trusted Root Certification Authorities). If you don't recognize it, delete it.
audit.rootcerts.found: {n} root certificate(s) in your user store
audit.recent_exes.title: Recent executables in AppData and Temp
audit.recent_exes.why: Droppers and infostealers drop themselves in %AppData%, %Temp% or Public and are usually unsigned.
audit.recent_exes.fix: Review the list; a known installer or updater is normal. Anything you don't recognize, upload it to VirusTotal.
audit.recent.found: {n} unsigned file(s) or script(s) from the last 14 days
audit.ifeo.blocks: {n} telemetry executable(s) blocked with taskkill (a typical debloater trick, not malware)
audit.can_fix: {n} of these findings can be fixed with Hardening (reversible, with a restore point).
audit.ask_fix: Open Hardening with those settings selected? [y/N]:

harden.subtitle: reversible security settings

harden.net.llmnr_off.title: Turn off LLMNR
harden.net.llmnr_off.desc: Stops Responder from stealing your NetNTLMv2 hash on shared networks.
harden.net.llmnr_off.breaks: almost nothing; only networks without DNS relying on broadcast names
harden.net.netbios_off.title: Turn off NetBIOS over TCP/IP
harden.net.netbios_off.desc: Closes NBT-NS, the other path Responder poisons.
harden.net.netbios_off.breaks: seeing very old machines by name on the local network
harden.net.firewall.title: Firewall on for all profiles
harden.net.firewall.desc: Turns on all three profiles and blocks unallowed inbound connections.
harden.net.firewall.breaks: services listening on your PC without a rule (you'll be asked)
harden.net.smb1_off.title: Remove SMBv1
harden.net.smb1_off.breaks: NAS or printers older than ~15 years
harden.net.remotereg_off.title: Disable Remote Registry
harden.net.remotereg_off.desc: Nobody can read or change your registry over the network.
harden.net.rdp_off.title: Turn off Remote Desktop
harden.net.rdp_off.desc: Closes one of ransomware's favorite entry points.
harden.net.rdp_off.breaks: connecting to this PC via RDP (Sunshine/Moonlight and Tailscale are not affected)
harden.net.smb_signing.title: Require SMB signing
harden.net.smb_signing.desc: Prevents NTLM relay and tampering with shared-folder traffic.
harden.net.smb_signing.breaks: cheap or old NAS that don't sign; network file copies slightly slower
harden.iso.wdigest_off.title: Turn off WDigest
harden.iso.wdigest_off.desc: Windows won't keep your password in plaintext in memory.
harden.iso.lsa_ppl.title: LSA protection (RunAsPPL)
harden.iso.lsa_ppl.desc: LSASS becomes a protected process: mimikatz can no longer read its credentials.
harden.iso.lsa_ppl.breaks: some anti-cheats, old drivers or unsigned LSA plugins (if a game stops launching, undo it)
harden.iso.hvci.title: Memory integrity (HVCI)
harden.iso.hvci.desc: Blocks vulnerable or malicious kernel drivers.
harden.iso.hvci.breaks: VirtualBox switches to Hyper-V and gets SLOWER (your Kali/Parrot VMs); some anti-cheats, overclock/RGB tools and old drivers stop loading; some gaming performance
harden.iso.credguard.title: Credential Guard
harden.iso.credguard.desc: Isolates credentials in a virtualized environment.
harden.iso.credguard.breaks: same as HVCI with VirtualBox; also NTLMv1 and DES Kerberos stop working
harden.sys.smartscreen.title: Turn on SmartScreen
harden.sys.smartscreen.desc: Warns before opening unknown or malicious downloaded programs.
harden.sys.smartscreen.breaks: nothing; you'll just see a (skippable) warning for uncommon programs
harden.sys.uac_max.title: UAC: always notify
harden.sys.uac_max.desc: Asks on the secure desktop for Windows' own changes too.
harden.sys.uac_max.breaks: nothing; a few more UAC prompts
harden.sys.autorun_off.title: Turn off AutoRun for all drives
harden.sys.autorun_off.desc: Nothing runs by itself when a USB or disc is plugged in.
harden.sys.autorun_off.breaks: the automatic menu when inserting a disc
harden.sys.pslog.title: PowerShell script logging
harden.sys.pslog.desc: Records what PowerShell runs in Event Viewer (useful to investigate an infection).
harden.sys.pslog.breaks: nothing; the event log takes a bit more space
harden.sys.psv2_off.title: Remove PowerShell 2.0
harden.sys.psv2_off.desc: Removes the AMSI-less version malware uses to dodge the antivirus.
harden.sys.psv2_off.breaks: very old scripts that ask for -version 2
harden.sys.lock.title: Lock after 15 minutes of inactivity
harden.sys.lock.desc: If you walk away without locking, the PC locks itself.
harden.sys.lock.breaks: nothing; while you play or watch video there is activity and it doesn't lock
harden.sys.office_macros.title: Block macros in files from the internet
harden.sys.office_macros.desc: Word, Excel and PowerPoint won't run macros from downloaded documents.
harden.sys.office_macros.breaks: macros in downloaded templates (they can be unblocked per file)
harden.sys.wsh_off.title: Turn off Windows Script Host
harden.sys.wsh_off.desc: No .vbs/.js runs on double-click: a common malicious attachment vector.
harden.sys.wsh_off.breaks: some installers and admin scripts that use VBScript
harden.def.pua.title: Block potentially unwanted apps
harden.def.pua.desc: Defender blocks adware, bundled miners and junk-laden installers.
harden.def.pua.breaks: some pentest or “cracked” tools are flagged as PUA
harden.def.asr.title: ASR rules in audit mode
harden.def.asr.desc: Turns on 14 attack surface reduction rules in LOG-ONLY mode (they don't block). Check Event Viewer for a few weeks, then switch to blocking.
harden.def.asr_block.title: ASR rules in block mode
harden.def.asr_block.desc: Blocks Office spawning processes, obfuscated scripts, LSASS theft, WMI persistence, vulnerable drivers…
harden.def.asr_block.breaks: complex legitimate Office macros, some dev/pentest tools that read LSASS or spawn unusual processes
harden.mem.small_dumps.title: Small memory dumps
harden.mem.small_dumps.desc: After a blue screen a small dump is saved (still useful for diagnosis) instead of kernel memory.
harden.mem.small_dumps.breaks: deep blue-screen diagnosis (you can switch back to “automatic”)
harden.mem.clear_pagefile.title: Clear the pagefile at shutdown
harden.mem.clear_pagefile.desc: Overwrites pagefile.sys at shutdown so no secrets stay on disk. Not needed with BitLocker.
harden.mem.clear_pagefile.breaks: shutdown takes longer (with a 14 GB pagefile, quite a bit longer)
harden.mem.hiber.title: Turn off hibernation
harden.mem.hiber.desc: Deletes hiberfil.sys (a copy of RAM) and frees its space.
harden.guide.bitlocker.title: BitLocker with a startup PIN
harden.guide.bitlocker.steps:
It's what protects you most against theft or loss. Mapache doesn't turn it on by itself: if you lose the recovery key, you lose the disk.
1. First decide where you'll keep the recovery key (Microsoft account, USB or paper) OFF this PC.
2. Control Panel → BitLocker Drive Encryption → Turn on BitLocker for C: (Windows Pro). On Home: Settings → Privacy & security → Device encryption.
3. For the PIN (Pro): gpedit.msc → Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → BitLocker Drive Encryption → Operating System Drives → “Require additional authentication at startup” → Enabled → “Require startup PIN with TPM”.
4. In an admin console: manage-bde -protectors -add C: -TPMAndPIN   (it will ask for the PIN).
5. Verify: manage-bde -status C:   or run Mapache's audit again.
Before a BIOS update: manage-bde -protectors -disable C: -RebootCount 1 (otherwise it will ask for the recovery key).
harden.guide.secureboot.title: Secure Boot
harden.guide.secureboot.steps:
It's enabled in the BIOS/UEFI, not from Windows.
1. Check the disk is GPT: in PowerShell, Get-Disk | Select Number, PartitionStyle. If it's MBR, it must be converted first (mbr2gpt /validate /allowFullOS then /convert): back up first.
2. Restart and enter UEFI (Del/F2). On MSI boards: Settings → Advanced → Windows OS Configuration → BIOS UEFI/CSM Mode = UEFI, and Secure Boot = Enabled.
3. If it asks for keys, choose installing the factory keys (Install default keys / Standard).
4. Verify in Windows: msinfo32 → “Secure Boot State: On”, or Mapache's audit.
Note: your VirtualBox VMs aren't affected. A dual-boot Linux does need a signed shim (Ubuntu/Fedora ship one).
harden.guide.wu.title: Windows Update
harden.guide.wu.steps:
Being up to date matters more than any setting in this list.
1. Settings → Windows Update: does it say “paused”? Click “Resume updates”.
2. Win+R → services.msc → “Windows Update”: the startup type must not be “Disabled”.
3. If you use AtlasOS or another debloater, check its options (in Atlas, the C:\Windows\AtlasDesktop folder) in case it disabled or deferred updates.
4. Check for updates and install the pending cumulative ones; restart.
5. Verify with Mapache's audit (the date of the last update).
harden.guide.defender_exclusions.title: Review Defender exclusions
harden.guide.defender_exclusions.steps:
Mapache doesn't delete exclusions by itself: you may have added some on purpose (pentest tools).
1. In an admin PowerShell: Get-MpPreference | Select-Object Exclusion*
2. For each one you don't recognize: Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "path"  (or -ExclusionProcess / -ExclusionExtension).
3. If you exclude your tools, keep it to one specific folder (e.g. D:\Tools\pentest), never Downloads, AppData, Temp or a whole drive.
harden.guide.standard_account.title: A standard account for daily use
harden.guide.standard_account.steps:
With a standard account, whatever you run (a mod, a crack) can't touch the system without the admin password.
1. Settings → Accounts → Other users → Add account (it can be local).
2. Keep it as “Standard user” and use it daily; the admin one only to install.
3. Games and Steam work the same; UAC will ask for the admin password when needed.

privacy.title: PRIVACY
privacy.subtitle: telemetry, ads and browsers (reversible)
privacy.menu_apply.desc: Shows the missing privacy settings (Windows and your browsers) and what they change. Restore point and previous value of everything.
privacy.menu_guides.desc: What a Windows program can't do for you, explained without hype.
privacy.hint: BASIC items come checked (they don't break anything important). Advanced ones change something you may use: read them.
privacy.all_done: ✓ All available privacy settings are already applied.
privacy.win.telemetry.title: Windows telemetry at minimum
privacy.win.telemetry.desc: Diagnostic data at the lowest level your edition allows (Home/Pro: "Required"; Enterprise/Education: "Security") and no feedback surveys
privacy.win.telemetry.breaks: nothing in normal use; the Insider Program needs optional data
privacy.win.adid.title: Advertising ID off
privacy.win.adid.desc: Apps no longer get a unique identifier to profile you for ads
privacy.win.adid.breaks: nothing; in-app ads stop being personalized
privacy.win.activity.title: Activity history off
privacy.win.activity.desc: Windows stops recording which apps, files and sites you open (and uploading it)
privacy.win.activity.breaks: "pick up where you left off" across devices
privacy.win.tailored.title: No "tailored experiences"
privacy.win.tailored.desc: Microsoft doesn't use your diagnostic data for tips, suggestions and offers
privacy.win.start_ads.title: No ads in Start or Explorer
privacy.win.start_ads.desc: Removes suggested apps in Start, recommendations/tips, apps that install themselves (Candy Crush & co.) and OneDrive nags in Explorer
privacy.win.lock_ads.title: No ads on the lock screen
privacy.win.lock_ads.desc: Removes "fun facts, tips and more" from the lock screen
privacy.win.websearch.title: Start search without Bing
privacy.win.websearch.desc: What you type in Start is no longer sent to Bing; it only searches your PC
privacy.win.websearch.breaks: web results inside the Start menu
privacy.win.typing.title: Typing and inking without collection
privacy.win.typing.desc: Windows stops harvesting what you type and draw to "personalize" the dictionary
privacy.win.typing.breaks: text suggestions learn less from you
privacy.win.recall.title: Recall off
privacy.win.recall.desc: Recall saves screenshots of everything on screen (passwords, chats…). It only exists on Copilot+ PCs; the policy blocks it if an update brings it
privacy.web.telemetry.title: Browsers: telemetry off
privacy.web.telemetry.desc: Policies so Edge, Brave and Firefox (the installed ones) don't send stats or run experiments. Chrome only accepts that policy on domain-joined PCs: turn it off in Settings → Privacy
privacy.web.telemetry.breaks: nothing; the browser will say "Managed by your organization" (that's the policy, not a virus)
privacy.web.ads.title: Browsers: no browser advertising
privacy.web.ads.desc: Edge: shopping, Rewards and recommendations. Firefox: sponsored shortcuts and stories
privacy.web.ads.breaks: nothing; the browser will say "Managed by your organization"
privacy.web.webrtc.title: Chromium browsers: WebRTC without IP leaks
privacy.web.webrtc.desc: WebRTC only uses the default public interface: with a VPN it doesn't reveal your real or local IPs
privacy.web.webrtc.breaks: rarely, video calls on very restrictive networks
privacy.web.cookies.title: Browsers: block third-party cookies
privacy.web.cookies.desc: Cuts cross-site tracking with cookies (Firefox already isolates them by default)
privacy.web.cookies.breaks: some embedded logins, chats and payments; can be allowed per site
privacy.web.doh.title: Browsers: encrypted DNS (Quad9)
privacy.web.doh.desc: DNS queries go encrypted to Quad9 (non-profit, no IP logging, blocks malware domains): your ISP or public wifi no longer see which sites you visit through DNS
privacy.web.doh.breaks: local network names, public wifi captive portals and DNS-based parental/corporate filters
privacy.web.suggest.title: Browsers: no search suggestions
privacy.web.suggest.desc: What you type in the address bar is no longer sent, keystroke by keystroke, to the search engine
privacy.win.location.title: Location off system-wide
privacy.win.location.desc: No app (nor Windows) can query your location
privacy.win.location.breaks: Find my device, local weather, maps and automatic time zone
privacy.win.clipboard.title: Clipboard not synced to the cloud
privacy.win.clipboard.desc: What you copy (passwords included) isn't uploaded to your Microsoft account
privacy.win.clipboard.breaks: pasting on another device what you copied on this one
privacy.guide.fingerprint.title: Fingerprinting: what CAN'T be done from Windows
privacy.guide.fingerprint.steps:
The fingerprint is computed INSIDE the browser: canvas, fonts, GPU, resolution, time zone…
No Windows program (Mapache included) can "hide" it. Distrust anything that promises to.
Paradox: unusual settings make you MORE unique. The real defense is looking like many others:
· Mullvad Browser or Tor Browser: every user has the same fingerprint.
· Brave: randomizes the fingerprint per site.
· Firefox with resistFingerprinting (arkenfox enables it).
Check your fingerprint at coveryourtracks.eff.org
privacy.guide.browsers.title: Choosing and configuring the browser
privacy.guide.browsers.steps:
Most private → least: Mullvad Browser / Tor > Brave > Firefox with arkenfox > Firefox > Edge/Chrome.
Firefox + arkenfox (github.com/arkenfox/user.js):
1. Close Firefox. about:profiles → open your profile's root folder.
2. Copy user.js there (and optionally user-overrides.js with your exceptions).
3. Read the wiki first: arkenfox clears cookies on close and breaks some sites on purpose.
Recommended extension in any browser: uBlock Origin (blocks ads and trackers).
privacy.guide.edition.title: Why telemetry doesn't reach 0 on Home/Pro
privacy.guide.edition.steps:
Microsoft only honors the "Security" level (0) on Enterprise, Education and Server.
On Home and Pro the real minimum is "Required" (1): device and reliability data, not your content.
Mapache writes the honest value for your edition instead of pretending to set 0.
See what is sent: Settings → Privacy → Diagnostics → "Diagnostic Data Viewer".
privacy.guide.permissions.title: Camera, microphone and app permissions
privacy.guide.permissions.steps:
Settings → Privacy & security → App permissions.
1. Camera and Microphone: keep only the apps that really use them (Discord, OBS…).
2. Check "Recent activity" in each: it shows which app used them and when.
3. Documents, Pictures, Contacts, Email: deny Store apps that don't need them.
The taskbar shows an icon whenever an app is using the camera, microphone or location.
privacy.guide.account.title: Microsoft account, OneDrive and sync
privacy.guide.account.steps:
With a Microsoft account, Windows syncs wifi passwords, settings and (with OneDrive) Desktop/Documents.
· Settings → Accounts → Windows backup: choose what syncs.
· OneDrive → Settings → Backup: decide whether Desktop/Documents/Pictures are uploaded.
· Your BitLocker recovery key is stored in your account: convenient, but Microsoft has it.
A local account avoids almost all of this, at the cost of losing sync.
privacy.guide.services.title: Why Mapache doesn't disable services or edit "hosts"
privacy.guide.services.steps:
Many "privacy tools" turn off DiagTrack, block Microsoft domains in hosts or delete system tasks.
That breaks Windows Update, the Store or Defender in ways that are hard to diagnose, and doesn't undo cleanly.
Mapache only uses documented policies (the same as Group Policy): they do the same and revert exactly.
If you want network-level blocking, a blocking DNS (NextDNS, AdGuard DNS, Pi-hole) that you can turn off is better.
optimize.title: OPTIMIZATION
optimize.subtitle: only what actually helps (reversible)
optimize.menu_apply.desc: Startup programs, third-party tasks and power plan: what each does and what changes. Everything undoes just like Hardening.
optimize.menu_guides: Guides (what we DON'T do, bloatware, drivers, power)
optimize.menu_guides.desc: What "optimizers" promise and don't deliver, and what is worth doing by hand.
optimize.hint: Only BASIC items come checked. Startup programs and tasks are your call: disabling uninstalls nothing, it just stops them from starting on their own.
optimize.all_done: ✓ Nothing pending: startup, tasks and power are already as they should be.
optimize.startup.breaks: the program no longer opens by itself at sign-in (you open it when you need it); same as disabling it in Task Manager
optimize.tasks.breaks: the program stops doing that task on its own (re-enable it with Undo)
optimize.power.not_saver.title: Leave the "Power saver" plan
optimize.power.not_saver.desc: On a desktop, "Power saver" caps CPU frequency and slows games and builds. Switches to "Balanced", which boosts fully when needed and idles down. (Choosing another plan, like AtlasOS's, also counts)
optimize.power.not_saver.breaks: nothing; the PC draws a bit more under load
optimize.game.bg_recording.title: No background game recording
optimize.game.bg_recording.desc: Xbox Game Bar can continuously record the last minutes of gameplay: that does cost performance (it encodes video all the time)
optimize.game.bg_recording.breaks: "Record what happened" (Win+Alt+G); manual capture still works
optimize.storage.sense.title: Turn on Storage Sense
optimize.storage.sense.desc: Windows removes unused temporary files and, by default, anything older than 30 days in the Recycle Bin. Downloads is NOT touched unless you configure it
optimize.storage.sense.breaks: Recycle Bin files older than 30 days are deleted automatically
optimize.guide.dont.title: What Mapache does NOT do (and why)
optimize.guide.dont.steps:
· Registry cleaning: speeds up nothing (Microsoft doesn't support it) and can break programs.
· "Freeing RAM": free RAM is wasted RAM; Windows uses it as cache and releases it when needed. Emptying it makes everything SLOWER.
· Blindly disabling services: breaks Windows Update, printers, Bluetooth or the Store, and saves almost nothing.
· "Network tweaks" (TCP, Nagle…): Windows 10/11 auto-tuning is already good; magic values usually make it worse.
· Promising FPS: what matters most in a game is the GPU, its drivers and the game's own graphics settings.
optimize.guide.bloat.title: Bloatware and Store apps
optimize.guide.bloat.steps:
Removing apps is UNINSTALLING, not a reversible setting: that's why it lives in the Programs module.
1. Main menu → Programs → search with / (Candy Crush, TikTok, Clipchamp…).
2. "Provisioned" apps get reinstalled for new users: Programs flags them.
3. Do NOT remove: Microsoft Store, App Installer (winget), Windows Security, WebView2, VC++/.NET runtimes.
optimize.guide.drivers.title: Drivers: what actually gives performance
optimize.guide.drivers.steps:
1. GPU: driver from the NVIDIA/AMD/Intel site or app, not Windows Update's (usually old).
2. Chipset: AMD's or Intel's for your board (improves CPU power management).
3. In the BIOS: enable XMP/EXPO so RAM runs at its rated speed (many PCs leave it at half).
4. Monitor: check in Settings → Display → Advanced that the refresh rate is the maximum (144/165 Hz…).
optimize.guide.power.title: Power plans, without myths
optimize.guide.power.steps:
· Balanced: boosts the CPU fully when needed. It's what Microsoft, AMD and Intel recommend for almost everyone.
· High / Ultimate performance: keep the CPU from clocking down. Small gains (sometimes 1–3 % in some game), more power and heat.
· Power saver: caps the CPU. Only makes sense on a laptop low on battery.
Change it: Win+R → powercfg.cpl
optimize.tasks.breaks_medium: ⚠ it's an UPDATER: you'll stop getting automatic updates, security ones included; update it by hand or re-enable it with Undo
